Entertainment.title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
Entertainment.text:
For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.

Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.

Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.

And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do.

"They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.

He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else.

"They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May.

"The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."

Engelsman says they themselves initially had many of the same doubts that viewers will have.

"We've had all the same reactions that the audience has had to every part of this process like, 'Who would do that? What an idiot.'

"We've been through it all and we're just lucky enough to have come out the other side and realised, 'OK, this is actually all stuff that could work.'"

"Now we've filmed it, I'm just excited to show the world," Bourgeois says. "We've done our absolute best and the critics will be critics and I hope that we will prove them wrong."

Holland adds that he hopes people will give the show a chance before judging.

"Have a watch and if you don't like it, you're well within your rights, I can't force anyone to like anything."

For a show built around the chemistry of its three former presenters, finding a replacement trio with such chemistry was always going to be as important as finding people who knew about cars.

Engelsman and Holland are an already established double act as the presenters of Throttle House, a motoring YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers.

The bigger unknown was who would become their third presenter.

That search eventually led the show's producers to Francis Bourgeois, a social media star better known for standing on railway platforms than behind the wheel of a supercar.

Engelsman says he and Holland had done chemistry testing with a number of people, but Bourgeois immediately felt different.

"As soon as Francis showed up, we were like: 'That guy'," Holland says.

Bourgeois remembers their first meeting taking place on a leather sofa in a hotel outside Basingstoke, where they mostly talked about what cars they owned.

By the time filming began, Holland says there was no need to consciously work out how to make the three-person dynamic function as "it just worked and clicked immediately".

While the chemistry came quickly, actually finding out they had the job was much less straightforward. Engelsman says there was "no immediate moment" when they were formally told they had been chosen.

"It was the most gradual thing," he says.

He and Holland initially thought they were simply part of a wider audition process, but then found themselves repeatedly being invited into writers' rooms and asked for their views on ideas for the show.

For Bourgeois, that uncertainty may have been helpful as he admits he'd "just fall apart and start crying" if he'd found out about the job.

There is a clear generational shift with the new presenters, all three of whom built their profiles on social media - and critics have been mixed on how successfully that translates to The Grand Tour.

The Independent's three-star review, external described the reboot as "all rather safe" and said the presenters feel "stilted".

The Guardian's review, external agreed and called the trio a "decent, if slightly anonymous, presence" who seem "quite meek and pleasant, and without any obvious dynamic".

But it did praise Bourgeois, with Stuart Heritage calling him "the most enthusiastic enthusiast currently working on planet Earth".

The FT also awarded the show three-stars, external and said that while the big budget spectacles are enjoyable to watch, they also feel "a little muted".

It added that "the real question is whether a series that has been driven by big personalities like Clarkson, May and Hammond can survive with a new team".

Hammond tells BBC News he tuned in for The Grand Tour's return and said it was great to see the new team getting going.

"That's the most important thing for them is to make their show. We made our show and we're really good at being us. They're going to be really good at being them," he says.

Hammond says the audience need to "give them the chance" to show that.

Bourgeois may be best known for his ecstatic trainspotting videos but he says his love of cars goes back just as far.

Growing up near Willesden Junction in London, there were plenty of trains to watch, but he was also fascinated by the cars outside his home.

"There was a particular Mitsubishi Legnum VR-4 that was outside my parents' flat window and I just loved it," he tells me. "I suppose with my social media, I'm just showing one of my passions and I have really wanted to let out that car enthusiasm too.

"It's nice that these two sides of my very strong passions are in harmony together and it's been a real pleasure to drive some of the cars on The Grand Tour."

His enthusiasm for transport more generally has already rubbed off on his co-presenters who say they've become "very educated by Francis on many things during long walks and long drives".

Bourgeois is even lobbying for The Grand Tour to devote an episode to another of his interests: power stations. And he has found a surprisingly receptive audience in Clarkson.

When the new trio met their predecessors, Bourgeois says seeing Clarkson in person gave him "a flutter in my tummy" and the pair bonded, inevitably, over trains, before moving on to power stations, and a lengthy discussion about cheeseburgers.

Engelsman says all three former presenters were supportive of their successors and "were very paternal and caring about it".

"They all seemed quite excited for there to be a new iteration," Engelsman says, adding that Clarkson even told them: "We'll look after you".

Entertainment.title: Jay-Z: Stars join US rapper at long-awaited UK show
Entertainment.text:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife Beyoncé had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

The show's opening set the tone for the star-studded evening to follow, as British actor Sir Idris Elba kicked things off by performing the intro track to his 2007 album, American Gangster.

As Jay-Z took to the stage, he recalled coming to London in 1989 with his mentor Jaz-O and seeing "what was possible" and it became a "special" place in his career.

His return to the capital this time round was explosive, with the rapper rattling through a string of hits like Izzo (H.O.V.A.), On To The Next One and Song Cry.

Throughout the show, vintage video clips and moments from his early career played across a massive LED screen, while an orchestra and a few guitarists accompanied him on stage.

There was no sign of Rihanna or Alicia Keys, who both made appearances during the New York run for their collaboration tracks, but the crowd made up for their absence by chanting back their lyrics during Run This Town and Empire State of Mind.

Jay-Z also took a moment to thank his fans who have been there from the beginning, telling them that "music saved my life".

His reflective mood continued as he performed Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem) and Where I'm From, which explores his upbringing in the Marcy housing projects in Brooklyn, New York.

He cranked the energy back up for his 2011 hit No Church in the Wild, which was amplified by fiery pyrotechnics that radiated heat through the stadium.

Originally a collaboration with controversial rapper Ye, also known as Kanye West, Jay-Z left his voice in for the chorus but cut his verses out.

US DJ Khaled had a brief moment on stage while Jay-Z changed, but it was the appearance of London-born rapper Giggs which got the crowd erupting.

He appeared overwhelmed at one stage, his hand clutching his face, as he took in the packed crowd while performing his track Talkin Da Hardest alongside Jay-Z.

The surprise guests didn't stop there, as Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean from the 90s American hip-hop collective The Fugees reunited to perform their hit tracks Ready or Not, Killing Me Softly with His Song and Fu-Gee-La.

It was a full-circle moment for both them and Jay-Z as he recalled supporting them on their European tour.

The US rap superstar closed out the night with rousing renditions of Public Service Announcement (Interlude) and Numb/Encore, hailing it as a "legendary night" that he would "never forget".

The crowd appeared to agree as thousands praised him by holding up his famous diamond hand gesture.

Fans had travelled from across the UK and the world to see the rapper, including Prince Dean Sithole, who hailed Jay-Z as one of his role models.

"I think he's very impacting, especially for us black people because we don't get a lot of recognition," the 19-year-old from Leeds told BBC Newsbeat.

"Seeing him today shows that dreams are possible and you can be that person that you want to be."

Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, broke through with his 1996 debut album, but it was his third record, Vol. 2: Hard Knock Life, in 1998 which landed him the top spot in the US charts for the first time and a best rap album Grammy.

He went on to establish himself as one of the most influential figures in hip-hop, releasing 13 solo studio albums and several collaboration records, which have secured him 25 Grammy Awards.

He was also the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017, as well as being inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

Over the years, he has also become one of the most prominent music moguls in the world, with his company Roc Nation representing a host of top talent and, in recent years, it has been behind the Super Bowl half-time show.

In 2019, he was declared hip-hop's first billionaire by Forbes, having built an empire based on music, property, fashion and investments alongside his wife Beyoncé.

The power couple have three children, daughter Blue Ivy, 14, and nine-year-old twins, Rumi and Sir.

Entertainment.title: TV has never been so nerve-jangling: 10 years of the agonising Motherland
Entertainment.text:
If Uncut Gems was about the school run instead of gambling debts, it would look like Motherland. It is now 10 years since the BBC sitcom jangled the already frayed nerves of all parents watching and turned Anna Maxwell Martin into the most frazzled woman on television in the name of skewering middle-class motherhood.

Whether she was marching her children to buy school shoes the night before term started (“Don’t be closed. Pleeeeeaaaaase don’t be closed”) or having a meltdown at temporary traffic lights en route to a school drop-off that proved redundant because she’d forgotten it was half-term, Maxwell Martin’s Julia would undoubtedly have a more chilled-out time in the kitchen of The Bear than raising her kids.

Originally created by Sharon Horgan, Holly Walsh, Helen Serafinowicz and Graham Linehan (with Barunka O’Shaughnessy joining from series two, after Linehan departed), Motherland arrived into a TV landscape where mothers were no longer images of parenting perfection. But while the likes of Malcolm in the Middle and Outnumbered had embraced the humour in the warts and all of child-rearing, the experience of mothering on television was still mostly centred on the kids themselves: tantrumming toddlers, precocious primary schoolers and stroppy teenagers.

Motherland took a different tack. It was never about the offspring, who rarely amounted to more than the occasional school uniform bobbing into view (rare is a Motherland fan who can name all – or indeed any – of the sprogs). Instead, it was more like a workplace comedy, focusing on the adult experience of motherhood: the passive aggression, the barely disguised competition, the begged-for favours, the ulterior motives, the whingeing and the copious bottles of wine. While it had been considered progress to see women on television who were more than just mothers, Motherland acknowledged an uncomfortable truth: that the mothering bit can really take over, at least for a while there. That being a mother sometimes – often – feels like a constant fight against being flattened into two dimensions.

Alongside Maxwell Martin’s perma-stressed Julia was unflappable Liz (Diane Morgan), token dad Kevin (Paul Ready), long-suffering Anne (Philippa Dunne) and Amanda (Lucy Punch), a vividly heinous alpha-mum creation who always saw herself as the centre of the universe and now literally is, in spin-off Amandaland. The series two introduction of Meg (Tanya Moodie), a high-flying Black woman who appeared to have it all together, gave us a more diverse group but Motherland was carefully hyper-specific to its well-off west London demographic. The horrors here took place at interminable PTA fundraisers, joylessly non-competitive sports days and skin-crawling swimming pool birthday parties (devastatingly, not a drop-off situation).

In Motherland, panic rises faster than house prices in a good school catchment area, and there is always someone to witness you making a colossal balls-up such as panicking about forgetting World Book Day and sending your child in holding an umbrella … as the novel Umbrella by Will Self. Obviously.

The show gamely took on the utter weirdness of mother-to-mother relations: attempting variously to bond with, impress and one-up a group of people who just happen to have given birth around the same time as you. The thwarted efforts to join carpools and get your kids into after-school clubs, all the while doing just enough to appease this gaggle of onlookers eager to judge (if only to convince themselves they are doing OK).

Amanda may be the obvious villain, but Motherland never stopped reminding us that motherhood will, at times, make sinners of us all. Having children does not suddenly wash away our foibles; if anything, it probably magnifies them. Motherland understood that being a mother frequently involves your spirit hovering somewhere above your body, watching yourself mutter Latin gibberish in an attempt to get your kids into a Catholic school, and silently screaming: “How did it come to this?”

As the series progressed and the bonds formed at the school gates transitioned into real friendships, the stakes got higher. But Motherland never lost sight of the relentless nature of parenthood: even as divorce, illness and death reared their heads, lunches still had to be packed (and probably left at home).

It’s a show that really should have had parents diving for the remote rather than spend their evenings reliving a hellish half-term cottage break or attempting to curb a nit epidemic. As Julia hissed when she ended up back at Anne’s house for an afterparty (a special bottle of cava and some dubious homemade paté): “This is my worst nightmare come true – surrounded by mums at night.”

But while it’s too close to the bone to be a comfort watch, sitting down in front of Motherland is an act of catharsis – a reassurance that even when you’re trying really really hard, you still might lose someone else’s child while trick-or-treating. If you no longer identify as a Carrie or a Samantha, perhaps being a Liz or a Kevin feels more appropriate.

It stands up as a triumphantly messy monument to a stage of life that passes in a blur of doctor’s appointments and sponsored bike rides and forgotten swimming kits. Less laugh till you cry and more laugh to stop yourself crying, Motherland holds out a hand to mothers watching. Not to help, of course, but to cling on to across a pub table as you try to fathom how on earth you’ve agreed to sort out the collection for the school’s poorly caretaker.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK government expected to announce restrictions on trade with West Bank settlements
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The UK government is to set out new restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the BBC understands.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to outline the measures in the Commons on Tuesday, which could include restrictions on trade in agricultural products from settlements.

Last week, Miliband said he would unveil a "comprehensive reset" of the British government's policy on Israel.

The Israeli government has previously warned it would retaliate if any new measures were introduced.

Settlements are illegal under international law, and recent months have seen a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers.

One minister told the BBC: "The statement will be a complete reset of the nature of our Israel-Palestine relationship. It will all feel very different.

"It is not just about sanctions. We hope that this will finally achieve what those of us who have been working towards for two years over the Middle East have been working on."

BBC News has not seen the full details of the measures.

But Labour MPs who have been briefed on the plans believe the sanctions will target trade with illegal settlements. They believe that means the sanctions would cover both goods and services.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed to Labour MPs at their weekly parliamentary meeting on Monday night that Miliband would be making the statement, according to a number of MPs present.

The prime minister is also said to have told the meeting that he had briefed international leaders about plans in phone calls on Monday afternoon.

Burnham spoke to US President Donald Trump over the phone on Monday, during which the prime minister stressed the importance of a two-state solution in the Middle East.

An official account of the call released by No 10 did not specify that Burnham had briefed Trump on the sanctions, while the US - which is likely to strongly oppose the proposals - has not commented.

Speaking in July, Stephen Doughty - who was then Europe minister but has since been appointed Middle East minister - told the business select committee that existing powers to impose restrictions on settlements did not go far enough.

He said: "At the moment, we can sanction where there is evidence of it being linked to settler violence, but not, for example, in relation to a contractor working on the settlements. We need to expand our sanctions powers."

While ministers are said to recognise that banning a relatively small quantity of mostly agricultural products is a largely symbolic gesture, the government is expected to frame this announcement as a major reset in Britain's wider policy on Israel.

The expected announcement by the UK government comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.

Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Police seek to identify protesters behind Portsmouth anti-migrant disorder
BreakingNewsTab.text:
How many people cross the English Channel in small boats?

Between 1 January and 6 September 2026, a total of 17,138 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 7 September 2025 to 6 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will not be working royals allowed to carry out official engagements now they have returned to the UK, a letter sent on behalf of King Charles spells out.

The letter is intended to clarify the status of Prince Harry and Meghan, who moved back from California with children Archie and Lilibet last month.

They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.

It comes as Prince Harry appears to have been pictured for the first time since his return, with a photo on social media showing him at a London TV and podcast studio.

The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.

Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.

This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.

It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.

This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.

The couple have kept a low profile, but the first picture of Prince Harry since coming back to the UK appears to have been posted on the social media account of Tower Bridge Studios in London.

The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.

This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals.

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.

The letter sent on behalf of the King makes it clear that this remains the case.

"The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it adds.

The King's message says that any questions from organisations about the reception to be given to the Sussexes, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow
BreakingNewsTab.text:
On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshly installed barbed wire fencing and reinforced school gates as the sun began creeping through olive trees around the village, deep inside the occupied West Bank.

"We are scared," Bassam al Assaf told me. "The students are afraid, and their parents are afraid."

Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April.

"I was inside my classroom and two little students came rushing to tell me there were settlers close to the school wall," remembers English teacher Waheed Abu Naem, whose brother Jihad was also killed by an Israeli soldier in the same attack.

Waheed said he was trying to move pupils to safety inside the school gate when the settler fired towards them. Mobile phone footage shows the moment Aws was shot.

"When I turned him onto his back, I saw lots of blood coming from his nose and mouth, and the bullet in his head," said Waheed. "We lost him."

He told me that bullets continued hitting the school building, as students hid behind the walls of their classrooms, or lay on the floor.

The Israeli military said in a statement at the time that stones had been hurled at a car carrying "civilians including a reservist soldier", and that the reservist had got out of the vehicle and fired at suspects.

Israeli media reported the reservist was later suspended from duty and an investigation launched.

Since that day, the casualties have grown alongside parents' fears.

Over the summer, two more pupils were shot dead by Israeli forces during settler attacks and incursions in the village, along with a 19-year-old who had just left the school.

In both cases, Israel's army said its forces responded to instigators of "a violent riot".

With three empty desks in the classrooms, some parents were reluctant to send their children back for the new school year.

The school sits right on the edge of Al-Mughayyir, an isolated village north-east of Ramallah, increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.

Bassam al-Assaf has installed a long barbed-wire fence around the compound and reinforced the school gates, to try and reassure parents. Ambulance crews are now stationed on the road outside, and several parents have volunteered to wait outside the school all day as an extra layer of protection.

"I came because it makes the children feel their parents are with them, that they are safe, it gives them a kind of security," said Haroon Bishara, whose boys are in the first and second grades.

"We fear for our children more this year," he told me. "We know the situation is not safe at the school."

But he said that fear was mixed with a determination not to let the threat from settler attacks force them out.

Lined up in the playground for their first assembly, pupils heard the instructions repeated by teachers again and again throughout the day: if soldiers or settlers approach the school, don't shout, don't go near them, don't react.

Just over an hour after classes began, settlers were spotted through the school windows: two men, driving sheep through Palestinian fields a couple of hundred metres from the school, as Israeli soldiers stood close by.

Minutes later, another settler with a flock of sheep appeared.

"They have got closer to the village since April," said Abu Naem. They used to keep their sheep behind this [hill], but now the soldiers bring the settlers up to the village."

We asked the Israeli army for its response to all the allegations in this report, but they were unable to provide one before publication.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.

But one of the ambulance crews stationed outside the school said that, rather than remove illegal settlements, Israeli soldiers had begun supporting and enabling settler incursions into the village.

Hadi al-Naasan, an ambulance driver in the village, said there had been a shift in the behaviour of Israeli forces over the past year. And that the rise in Palestinian deaths and injuries in al-Mughayyir this year reflected that.

"At the beginning of 2025, settler attacks were few, due to the army's interventions," he said. "In 2026, the situation changed completely: the settlers became fully protected by the occupation soldiers. This year, the number of martyrs is higher, the number of injuries is also much higher – and the number of child injuries is higher too."

Hadi, along with other residents of al-Mughayyir, believes that some Israeli settlers are now deliberately targeting children in order to put pressure on the adults in the village to leave their homes.

A UN Commission of Inquiry published in June found that settler attacks "have instrumentalized children, external as part of a broader coercive strategy to drive Palestinians off their land."

And it described "a pattern of settlers intentionally targeting Palestinian children" while they were playing near their homes, walking to and from school, tending to farms or herding livestock, "turning everyday spaces into sites of fear".

Israel dismissed the report as a "libellous sham".

Sheep farmer Sami Abu Rahma firmly believes that some violent settlers are targeting children.

At the end of July, his nine-year-old son Salim was shot and injured as he played with his siblings on the family sheep farm outside al-Mughayyir. The bullet is still lodged in his arm.

Footage from security cameras at the farm shows Salim pointing, and shouting to his parents that settlers are approaching, before running for shelter with his siblings and mother, as two gunshots are heard. Salim is seen grabbing his shoulder.

"In that moment, you stop thinking; you just feel fear," Sami told me. "Fear that, God forbid, [the attacker] was shooting to kill. The first thing in your mind is losing the most precious thing you have."

The man who shot his son, he said, lived in an illegal settler outpost that appeared next to the farm in June – and had previously shot at Salim in the same area a week before.

"You no longer feel you can keep them safe in the street, or even at school," he said. "The settlers don't want us to stay here, [they want us to feel] as if there's no future for us here."

Sami said he was the last sheep farmer left in the area, the others all chased away by settler attacks. The settler who shot his son had told the family repeatedly to leave their land, he said.

"No matter how determined you might be to stay," he added, "what do you do when settlers start shooting your kids?"

The regional settlers council told us that an off-duty soldier was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the shooting.

"We regret any harm to innocent people, Jews or Arabs, and oppose any act of violence that violates the law," it said in a statement, adding that it rejected "the attempt to attribute to the entire settlement community in Judea and Samaria acts that have not yet been determined by an investigation, as well as the baseless claim that lawful sheep grazing or Jewish presence in the area are part of a deliberate plan to harm children or drive residents from their homes."

Al-Mughayyir is part of a pattern unfolding across the occupied West Bank, with more illegal settler outposts encircling Palestinian villages, more protection for settlers from Israeli forces, and attacks moving from farms and grazing land to built-up areas, where women and children are more at risk.

"Children, seeing the army enter, don't grasp the gravity of the situation," said the local ambulance crew, Hadi al-Naasan. "Adults are more aware of how events can unfold."

UN figures suggest that the number of Palestinians injured during settler attacks by Israeli soldiers or settlers has risen sharply this year to an average of three injuries per day, and that the number of injuries inflicted directly by settlers themselves is also higher.

This rise has been accompanied by an expansion of Israeli settlements and settler outposts in the West Bank.

All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, and Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government is under growing international pressure - including from the UK, which is expected to announce sanctions this week in response to Israeli settlement policies.

The arrest of some violent settlers and a reported plan by Israel's prime minister to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank have not so far stopped attacks, nor reassured Palestinians who say outposts previously demolished by Israeli authorities were quickly rebuilt.

With Israeli elections less than two months away, Israel's Finance Ministry pushed forward plans this week to take over land registration in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, described by the Israeli settlement monitor Peace Now as "a clear step towards annexation".

Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has attributed settler violence to a tiny extremist minority, describing them in a recent television interview as "150 juvenile delinquents".

Since the beginning of 2025, the UN has recorded 316 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 5,600 injured, to the end of July 2026. It says 20 Israelis were killed over the same period, including one child and eight members of the security forces, and 123 Israelis injured.

Palestinian parents who have stayed in villages like al-Mughayyir through escalating settler violence are now facing a growing fear of losing their children if they stay on their land.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Self-described 'racist monster' Thomas Webster jailed after BBC investigation
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Warning: This article contains graphic accounts of racist and violent language

A former tax worker who described himself as "the ultimate genocidal racist monster" has been jailed for inciting hatred online after he was exposed by a BBC investigation.

Thomas Webster was sacked by HMRC and investigated by police after comments he made to an undercover journalist in the BBC programme 'Unmasked: Extreme Far Right'.

Webster, 29, from Lapworth, Warwickshire, admitted 10 counts of stirring up racial hatred online, including ones calling for the killing and extinction of his racial "enemies".

Webster also admitted to stirring up religious hatred and another count of stirring up hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation. He was sentenced to two years at Warwick Crown Court.

In his online posts, Webster said he wanted Jewish and gay people to be tortured and executed.

Webster also said he wanted to kill all Muslims until they were "globally extinct."

In one instance, he said if a migrant hotel was placed on his road he would "prepare for murder and prison time, I am serious".

Webster was a member of the far right group Patriotic Alternative when BBC Wales Investigates' undercover reporter secretly recorded him at two of the group's events in 2024.

He was filmed saying that in his job at HMRC he liked to "deliberately" give non-white people "bad information which sounds interesting, like I'm deliberately trying to sabotage them."

Webster was dismissed by HMRC in February 2025, a month after the programme was broadcast.

The HMRC said it took breaches of its standards "extremely seriously" and had "robust processes" in place to investigate concerns.

"Where standards are not met, we act decisively," HMRC said in a statement.

"Following an internal disciplinary process, the individual concerned was dismissed from HMRC and ceased to be employed by the department in February 2025."

Talking to an undercover BBC reporter, Webster self-identified as a "white totalitarianist" who believed in "a world where white becomes the default human race... all other races will be extinct."

Describing himself as "a guy who seeks trouble" while on a hike with other Patriotic Alternative members, he boasted that he would have "crushed [the] skulls" of a group of non-white men if they had walked near to him.

Following the BBC programme, police opened an investigation and linked Webster to several social media accounts, mainly on X.

He was arrested for inciting racial hatred in September 2025 and police used details on his phone and computer to confirm the accounts were his. He was charged in July and pleaded guilty last month.

A number of the offending posts were still visible on X in the weeks after Webster pleaded guilty, as well as dozens of others in which he used the most extreme racist language.

In these additional posts, which did not form part of the charges, Webster praised Adolf Hitler and the Nazis and told several prominent politicians that they should be killed or subjected to sexual violence.

In one of his X posts, Webster described himself as a "genocidal racist monster."

He described his wishes for people of several races to be killed and in one post said "the next Hitler will be a man like me!"

After BBC contacted X about the posts, they were taken down - but the company did not comment further.

Days before Webster's sentencing, BBC News found another active Substack account appearing to belong to him.

The account shared posts discussing Webster's arrest, as well as intimate details of his personal life.

It also included several comments about race, including one calling for the "total genetic extinction" of people from South Asia.

One comment claimed that these posts were made in spite of bail conditions heavily limiting Webster's internet use and explicitly preventing him from communicating via social media.

After the BBC contacted Substack about the content, most of the posts were taken down, although one for which Webster was charged is still visible. The company did not respond further.

"That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."

Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour.

"Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views.

"I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't send you to custody."

Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech."

"Expressing a wish for people to be killed… Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as well… and encouraging other people to express similar views.

"It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.

Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again.

"Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.

Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Prince George to start school at Eton College
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Prince George is taking another step in growing up with his first day at Eton College.

He is following in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, who also attended the historic school in Berkshire.

The 13-year-old prince will become a boarder at the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around £65,000 a year.

As the oldest child of Prince William and Catherine, George is second in line of succession to the throne.

There had been speculation about which school Prince George would attend when he finished at independent prep school Lambrook in Berkshire, with a number of private schools being suggested.

But a traditional option was chosen, with Prince George following his father, uncle Prince Harry, and great uncle Earl Spencer in attending Eton College.

Prince George will now become a boarder, with the school having 25 boarding houses, with each having approximately 55 pupils, looked after by residential staff headed by a house master.

The school is also not far from the prince's family home in Windsor.

"Some boys take to boarding like a fish to water; others take a minute to settle in," writes the Good Schools Guide about Eton College, which says the school provides each boy with a private single room.

Melanie Sanderson, the school guide's managing editor, said Eton has "spectacular facilities and spacious grounds".

"Yet despite its ancient buildings, it is a modern school with a progressive outlook.

"Most 13-year-old boys arriving there in September cannot possibly know what adult life holds for them.

"Prince George, however, faces a very particular future and his parents, with an unrivalled choice of schools available to them, have decided that an Eton education represents the best preparation for life as a modern working royal," she said.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK weather: Drought and hosepipe bans remain despite wettest week since early February
BreakingNewsTab.text:
In the last few days of August and start of September, more rain fell than any other week since early February, according to the Environment Agency.

Despite the change to more unsettled and wetter conditions, all of Wales and most of England remains in drought.

And water companies are reminding customers that temporary hosepipe bans are still in force despite the rainfall and decreased demand with the cooler weather.

More rain is in the forecast this week and while that will be welcome, sustained rainfall is needed to reverse drought conditions.

While we had a brief return of summer heat over the weekend for some, the weather since the start of September - and meteorological autumn - has been more unsettled.

According to figures from the Environment Agency (EA), in the week from 28 August to 3 September, rainfall totals ranged from 26mm in south-east England to 48mm in central England.

However, the National Drought Group said that water storage "continued to decline at most reservoirs".

There has been no change to the EA drought status or the temporary use bans in force across ten water company areas.

Which areas are under a hosepipe ban?

While there has been less demand for water due to the cooler and wetter weather, "further significant rainfall is needed" to return to normal conditions the EA suggests.

In the first week of September there has been a big variation in rainfall across the UK.

For parts of Scotland we've already seen half the average September rainfall in the first 7 days of the month.

Prestwick, South Ayrshire for example has had 47mm compared to the whole month average of 79mm - or 59% of the average.

However, southern England and south Wales have been largely dry with locations in East Sussex, Buckinghamshire and the Isle of Wight recording less than a millimeter of rain - or 1% of the average September rain.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.

The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.

JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.

Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.

"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.

JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.

The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save £1.7bn over the next two years.

JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.

He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack.

"It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.

Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.

In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.

In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to £22.9bn from £29bn in the previous two years.

Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.

"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.

He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party" in terms of electric vehicles.

Jaguar launched the I-PACE, a fully-electric SUV, in 2018. But the electric Range Rover announced last week will be its first electric vehicle launch since then.

Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Police forces failing investigation basics, report says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to His Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary (HMIC).

In her annual report, Michelle Skeer also said too many victims were not receiving the quality of service they should expect.

Forces continue to struggle when it comes to gathering evidence, identifying and progressing lines of inquiry, and keeping victims updated on their cases, she added.

There was progress in neighbourhood policing and in some of the work carried out by regional organised crime units that focus on offenders across multiple local police force boundaries, the report said.

The report continued that the greatest strength of policing is its workforce, with the vast majority of officers showing professionalism and courage.

HMIC inspects all 43 police forces in England and Wales on a two-year cycle.

Out of 13 forces assessed in the current cycle, including Merseyside, Cumbria, and Devon & Cornwall, none received a good or outstanding rating for investigating crime or providing a safe and lawful custody environment.

The other forces assessed were Suffolk, Staffordshire, Thames Valley, West Yorkshire, Northamptonshire, Surrey, Wiltshire, North Yorkshire, Humberside and Kent.

The report says "too many forces still weren't getting the basics right or providing the public with a consistently good service in the areas that matter most to victims".

Beyond weaknesses in investigations, the report also highlights gaps in how forces respond to the public, including delays in handling emergency and non-emergency calls, and in response times to incidents.

It also raises concerns about the safeguarding of victims, noting inconsistencies in recognising vulnerability and failure to properly deploy resources appropriately when people are reported missing.

Skeer said it was a "pivotal moment for policing" and said "there are still areas where performance is not good enough".

"If managed correctly, I firmly believe that reform presents a significant opportunity to deliver a better service for both the public and those working within policing," she added.

The HMIC report said that evolving crime and threats mean officers deal with more complex and resource-intensive cases.

But the government's planned reforms, including the creation of a National Police Service to take over counter-terror and fraud investigations could alleviate some of the pressure facing local units, Skeer wrote.

Policing minister Sarah Jones said: "Our plans will tackle the long-term challenges in the policing system and bring it into the modern day.

"We are investing in more neighbourhood policing, raising standards and making better use of technology to make sure local policing works for local people."

Responding to the report, the charity Victim Support said: "Police forces are undoubtedly under immense pressure, but they must get the basics right."

Chief executive Katie Kempen added: "It is unacceptable that victims and survivors are paying the price for police failings. Every victim of crime deserves to be treated with respect, to be given access to justice, and to have their needs identified and met."

Growing financial pressure is repeatedly pointed to as increasing the strain on police forces.

Cleveland's police's Chief Constable, Victoria Fuller, recently told the BBC her force has been understaffed and under resourced for years.

"The facts are the facts," she said.

"We have got the highest crime rate in the country. We've had the largest decrease in officers in the country since 2010.

"As a police force, if you were to look at the multiple indices of deprivation, our police force is number one. So we absolutely need more, we need more resources."

An extra £2m targeted funding has since been designated to help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime.

Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026-2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash.

The annual HMIC report comes just months after a different publication by the Police Leadership commission found the system for identifying and developing leaders was too weak, with chief constable roles in England and Wales often attracting a single suitable candidate.

The landmark independent review warned police leadership is not consistently of a high enough standard and requires a fundamental overhaul.

It also pointed to low morale and motivation within the service, recommending reformed recruitment and promotion processes.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Maryam Moshiri: BBC News presenter reveals she has blood cancer
BreakingNewsTab.text:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer.

Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's best-known anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease.

"It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said.

"I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.

Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.

It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision.

"I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said.

"Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease.

"The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."

As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.

Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out.

This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood.

"In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said.

"After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."

Later, The World Today presenter was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place.

"I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said.

"I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life.

"It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."

She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better".

The mother-of-three said she has had to adjust to life with her condition, sometimes not being able to attend family occasions or play with her children because she is exhausted.

"It's the kind of fatigue that is not like I'm just tired and I didn't get a good night's sleep, you feel like someone has removed your battery completely, and however much sleep you get makes no difference," she explains.

"Even though I feel the best I have in two years, I don't know how I'm going to be in six months, one year, two years.

"People with PV have a higher chance of stroke, heart attack or DVT, so it's something I always have to be aware of and make sure I mitigate."

Despite the fatigue, Moshiri has continued to travel across the world covering the biggest stories over the last two years for the BBC, anchoring from Qatar at the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, covering the selection of the new Pope from the Vatican and travelling to Greenland for Vice-President JD Vance's visit.

She credits her "supportive and helpful" husband Jonathan, management at the BBC and her children Iris, 13, Vivienne, 11 and Caspian, 9.

"It took me a long time to be able to tell them about this illness, because I don't want to worry them, but they have been so understanding. When I say things like 'mummy is too tired to play with you', they get it and they don't push it," she said.

Helen Rowntree, chief executive of Blood Cancer UK, said: "We're so grateful to Maryam for bravely sharing her story. When public figures speak openly about their diagnosis, it cuts through the silence that so often surrounds blood cancer – the UK's fifth most common cancer and third biggest cancer killer."

Rowntree said blood cancer can feel like a "silent" cancer as patients can present with vague, hard to spot symptoms, and highlighted that many with the disease manage their illness, treatment and side-effects alongside work and family life.

"We urgently need continued public and government support to fund the next generation of kinder, more effective treatments with fewer side-effects – so that more people with blood cancer can live well, spend less time dealing with the impact of treatment and be there for the moments that matter," she added.

"There is a lot of research going into blood cancer and scientific advancement to look forward to. Hopefully they'll be some sort of advancement that will help even more than these medications I've been given," Moshiri added.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Germany's AfD calls for parties to work with it after Saxony-Anhalt win
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections there.

Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.

While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say, I do not accept the vote of the people".

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was "deeply shocked" by the result, describing it as "seismic... not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously".

His party, the conservative CDU, saw its share of the vote almost halved to 17.2% in the state's preliminary results.

Merz said it was not possible to return to "business as usual", adding that the country needed "profound reforms" and the CDU needed to "reach people at an emotional level".

No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.

Von Storch said the state's results "were on the table and now democrats have to talk to [one] another. This is what democracy demands".

She added that if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".

Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".

The state's defeated premier, the CDU's Sven Schulze, also said the mandate to govern Saxony-Anhalt "now lies with the AfD".

Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.

The party's plans for Saxony-Anhalt, which include segregating child refugees into special classes and setting up a task-force to help detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, are highly controversial within Germany.

The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.

Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".

One idea being floated is an informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.

The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on immigration and backs importing Russian gas.

Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude.

"We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.

Another possibility - at least in theory - is a messy, minority coalition government led by the conservative CDU party. But that appears very unlikely.

There's also the prospect of another election to break the deadlock - an idea which has been mooted by Siegmund who has said he doesn't want to compromise on his policy goals.

The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.

They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.

Merz described the Saxony-Anhalt defeat as the worst the CDU had suffered "in years, if not decades", acknowledging that the results in upcoming regional elections in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin could have "increasing significance".

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally.

Commentators and political opponents called AfD's victory a watershed and break with the past.

"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters overnight. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the state's projected results on his Truth Social platform. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev then took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".

Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.

Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".

Asked about those who had expressed fears over the far-right party gaining power in the state, deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC that its supporters were afraid of "losing our economy, they are afraid of losing our inner security".

She said conservative voters were turning to alternative political parties because they were not being listened to.

She added that the party's detractors should: "Wake up and realise what happened in several other European states... The conservative parties will disappear from the landscape as it happened in Italy, as it's about to happen in the UK, as it might also happen in France".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Eiffel Tower shut by staff strike over female workers being moved for religious visit
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers and management said.

A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the landmark in the French capital on Saturday.

Staff union representative Diane Davoine says as they arrived at the monument, women were told to move.

"During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," she told Reuters. Davoine also said management had since apologised to workers over the incident.

"So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," Davoine said.

She added: "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again."

Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), the company that operates the monument in Paris, confirmed the delegation had asked the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women", according to the AFP news agency.

The firm told AFP that "these conditions should not have been accepted".

They added they "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women".

SETE president Ariel Weil said: "It is clearly not an acceptable practice.

"I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women."

The BBC has contacted the Union Confédération générale du travail (CGT) for a response.

BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in the suburbs of Paris.

In a statement on X, the BAPS temple in Paris said their trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".

It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".

On its website, BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.

It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said there would be an investigation into the circumstances of the visit.

"I am taking note of the anger expressed by the employees of the Eiffel Tower, and I want to tell them that their discontent is legitimate," he wrote on X.

"Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city. It must be applied everywhere, for everyone."

French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."

Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."

FinanceTab.title: Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US
FinanceTab.text:
President Donald Trump has warned Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it can no longer sell in the US unless it moves its manufacturing there.

"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank'."

The move comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours, and hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs are set to be imposed on $20bn (£14.7bn) worth of US goods.

In a statement, Bombardier underscored that it employed thousands of American workers and said it valued its partnerships with American companies.

The BBC has reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney's office for comment.

It is unclear how Trump intends to block Bombardier from doing business in the US.

The Montreal-based company already operates a factory in the US state of Kansas that builds special mission military planes, and employs 3,500 American workers.

It also operates sites in Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, DC and New Jersey.

About half of its fleet – 5,100 aircraft – is operated by Bombardier customers based in the US.

In a statement on Monday, Bombardier did not address Trump's threat directly, but said its operations "create tens of thousands of US jobs through the company's growing American footprint".

"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees," its statement said. "Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country."

Bombardier's jets are built at facilities in Canada, the US and Mexico, according to the company's website. They also comply with the North American free trade agreement signed by Trump during his first term, known as CUSMA in Canada and the USMCA in the US.

The company is one of Canada's largest, having contributed C$7.4bn ($5.4bn; £4bn) to the country's GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombardier.

It is also one of the largest employers in Quebec's manufacturing sector.

In a post on X on Monday, Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a source of pride" for her province and "a flagship of our economy".

She added that she has reached out to Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and offered her government's full support.

On Trump's threat, Fréchette wrote: "I will not respond to provocation with provocation."

"Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market."

Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed late last month after Canada walked away from the negotiating table, after which the US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of presenting last-minute terms that were "unfair" and "uneconomic", while US officials accused him of refusing to sign a deal for political reasons because of Trump's unpopularity in Canada - an accusation he denied.

FinanceTab.title: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling
FinanceTab.text:
Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal has overturned a key part of a landmark ruling in 2024 which found the retailer was wrong to pay its warehouse staff higher basic pay than shop floor workers for jobs of equal value.

More than 3,500 current and former employees, mainly women, had been set to share potentially more than £30m in back pay as a result of that judgement.

After Next's appeal, the law firm Leigh Day, which represents store workers, described the conclusion on basic pay as "disappointing" and said it will appeal the decision.

The tribunal accepted that Next was justified in paying higher rates because of recruitment and retention pressures for warehouse workers.

Next described the decision as a "landmark victory" succeeding on the "key issue of basic pay".

In a statement, it said: "The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for Next to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other.

"In this case, Next had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse operatives because of recruitment and retention pressures, which did not apply to the workforce in its stores. Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.

"The judgment affirms a principle at the heart of any effective employment market - that employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so."

Leigh Day said judges did uphold 2024 findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.

Next said it will now seek permission to appeal these decisions.

Both the original Employment Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal found there was no direct sex discrimination in Next's pay rates. Shop floor staff are predominantly women while warehouse workers are predominantly male.

Questions are now being asked about if this result could set a precedent across the industry. Tesco, Asda, Morrisons, and Sainbury's are all involved in similar long running claims and will be studying the findings closely.

FinanceTab.title: Why the 'Temu Range Rover' is such a threat to Jaguar Land Rover
FinanceTab.text:
Jaguar Land Rover's decision to shed 4,000 jobs comes after the carmaker has travelled down a very rough road.

The company has seen sales fall in all of its major markets and has been dealing with the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year.

At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future, in which it is likely to face intense competition from aggressively expanding Chinese brands.

Executives have now decided a major overhaul is needed.

One of the main concerns for JLR is China. Not so long ago, it was seen as a land of opportunity for western carmakers, where the rapidly expanding middle classes seemed to have an inexhaustible appetite for upmarket foreign-badged vehicles.

JLR, along with other European brands such as BMW, Audi and Mercedes Benz, was all too willing to meet that demand, at a time when the European market was extremely crowded and growth hard to find.

Today, things are very different. The past decade has seen rapid growth among domestic Chinese carmakers, firmly backed by their government, which has been determined to make the country a leading player in electric vehicles.

This has created an environment of intense competition, in which local manufacturers have rapidly raised the bar in terms of technology and development speed.

That, combined with a slowdown in the Chinese economy and a reduction in sales overall, has made China a much more difficult market for European brands.

JLR's Chinese sales fell from a high water mark of 146,000 cars in 2017 to just 62,400 in the last financial year. At the same time, competition and a new luxury car tax have hit profit margins.

All of this has resulted in a sharp fall in revenues from the region. JLR is not alone in this; the Volkswagen Group, for example, has also seen its earnings in China pummelled – a major factor in its decision to axe 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade.

The state of the Chinese market has had another consequence for European carmakers, including JLR. Faced with cut-throat competition at home, Chinese firms such as BYD and Chery have been flexing their muscles abroad.

They have been rapidly gaining market share in the UK and Europe – with Chery's Jaecoo 7, nicknamed the 'Temu Range Rover' the third best-selling car in this country over the first half of the year.

Analysts say traditional brands will face an uphill struggle to compete with new rivals, who can sell cars more cheaply and develop them more quickly.

The US is also a major market for JLR. In the year to the end of March 2025 it sold more than 120,000 cars there. The following year, that figure had fallen to just under 100,000.

Part of that could be attributed to the impact of the cyber attack, which heavily disrupted production in late 2025. It affected JLR worldwide and cost the company £1.9bn.

But sales and profits were also hit by the introduction of import tariffs by the US, and subsequent uncertainty over the levels of those tariffs. As automotive analyst Matthias Schmidt puts it, the company is "seeing a head-on hit each time a Land Rover rolls off a ship onto US soil".

JLR is now planning a partnership with Stellantis to build new Defender-badged vehicles in the US. These cars, which would be developed specifically for the US market, would not attract tariffs.

Then, there are energy costs, which affect JLR and its rivals. Carmakers and their suppliers are industrial businesses that use copious amounts of energy, and prices in the UK are among the highest in Europe.

According to Prof David Bailey of Birmingham Business School, "electricity is a fundamental input into modern industrial production".

"If producing a car in Britain is structurally more expensive because the energy required to manufacture it is substantially more expensive, Britain is effectively imposing a competitiveness tax on its own industry."

All of these challenges have come at a time when JLR has been ploughing money into the development of a new generation of electric vehicles. The first fruits of the £15bn programme were seen last week, with the official unveiling of the first electric Range Rover.

That was relatively uncontroversial – but so far the relaunch of Jaguar as an all-electric brand has been anything but. In late 2024 the company drove straight into the heart of the culture wars with a polarising advertising campaign that some saw as excessively "woke". The first actual car is due to make its public bow on 6 October – and it will be a pivotal moment for the company.

It is easy to see why JLR's chief executive PJ Balaji feels action is necessary to trim costs and make the company leaner. That is bad news for employees, with thousands of jobs to go and compulsory redundancies not being ruled out.

But the carmaker's network of suppliers are also being squeezed.

"JLR has been pushing hard for cost savings", one leading supplier told the BBC. "But those suppliers are also facing high energy costs and high employment costs…there's huge anxiety right now."
